title: A filter at every door
hook: Most people in India have never used your machine. How do you get them to buy one?

future.label: Trust
future.hint: How many homes know your name and keep coming back

intro.text: Bombay, 1982. The Tata group's Forbes company and Sweden's Electrolux start a new company together, and you run it. Your first product is the Euroclean vacuum cleaner. Most Indian homes have never seen one and still sweep with a broom. You must make families want the machine and trust your name before the money runs out.

d1.title: Shop shelf or living room?
d1.setup: Shops already sell India's fans and radios, and dealers can reach many towns at once. But your machine is new, so most shoppers have never seen one work. You have a small team and not much money.
d1.question: How do you sell your first machine?
d1.advisor: Shops can reach thousands of buyers, and dealers pay for their own space. Home visits are slower, and every visit costs us money.

options.label: Sell through appliance shops in big cities, and use newspaper ads to bring buyers in.
options.outcome: Dealers put your box on a shelf beside the fans. Shoppers look at it, but few understand why they need it, and dealers spend little time explaining. Most boxes sit there for months.
options.why: A product people have never used won't sell from a shelf. Someone has to ask how the family cleans today, and then show the answer. Remember: ask questions first, then listen.
options.better: Send salespeople into homes. Let them ask how the family cleans, then show the machine working there.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you put a new product on a shelf. People are more likely to buy after seeing it work.

options.label: Send young salespeople into homes and show the machine working, one family at a time.
options.outcome: You open no shops. Instead, your salespeople carry the machine into homes and switch it on there. The work is slow and hard. By 1987, you still have just one office in Bombay and 20 salespeople, and the company is struggling.
options.why: A new kind of product must be shown, not shelved. In a home, a salesperson can ask how the family cleans, listen to the answer, and then show the machine on their own floor. Remember: ask questions first, then listen more than you talk.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you took your machine into homes. A new product is easier to sell when people see it work for them.

options.label: Open a few showrooms in big cities, give live demos, and wait for buyers to come in.
options.outcome: The people who walk in like the demo, but not many come. Most families will not make a trip to see a machine they do not know they need.
options.why: Showing the machine was right, but you waited for buyers to come to you. People rarely go looking for something they've never heard of. Remember: go to the buyer, ask questions first, then show.
options.better: Take the demo into people's homes, where you can ask how they clean and show the machine on their own floor.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you waited for buyers to visit. Go to them instead.

text.text: It is the late 1980s. Your vacuum cleaners still sit in shops, and sales are thin. You add a second product, Aquaguard, a water purifier for the kitchen. This time, you hire salespeople to take it into homes.
It is the late 1980s. Your showrooms get only a few visitors a day. You add a second product, Aquaguard, a water purifier for the kitchen, and start sending salespeople into people's homes.
It is the late 1980s, and your salespeople now have a second machine to carry: Aquaguard, a water purifier for the kitchen. It is a new kind of product in India, and very few homes have one.

d2.title: "We boil water for free"
d2.setup: In home after home, families say the same thing. Boiling water costs almost nothing, so why pay a lot for a machine? Your purifier is costly for most families, and your salespeople are tired of hearing "no".
d2.question: How do you answer "too costly"?
d2.advisor: They have a point. Boiling is nearly free. If we cannot match free, maybe we should at least get much closer.

options.label: Keep the price. Show the fuel and time boiling takes, and what one illness can cost.
options.outcome: You keep the price and make your case, home by home. Over the years, you talk many Indian families out of boiling their tap water and into buying Aquaguard. By 2004, three of every four water purifiers sold in India are yours.
options.why: Boiling looks free, but it isn't: it costs fuel and time every day, and an illness costs far more. Remember: when they say "too costly", ask "compared to what?"
options.takeaway: In the 1980s you answered "too costly" by showing families what boiling really costs.

options.label: Keep the price. Let families pay a small sum each month, so the cost feels much lighter.
options.outcome: More families sign up because the monthly sum looks small. But many still wonder why they should pay at all when boiling works, and some stop paying halfway. Chasing payments takes up your team's time.
options.why: Easy payments help people who already want the machine. They don't answer the real doubt: why pay when boiling is free? Remember: when they say "too costly", ask "compared to what?"
options.better: Keep the price, and show what boiling really costs in fuel, time and doctor's bills. Then your price looks fair.
options.takeaway: In the 1980s you made the price easier to pay, but did not show families why it was worth paying.

options.label: Cut the price by a third so more families can buy, even if you earn less on each sale.
options.outcome: More families buy, but each sale now barely covers your salesperson's pay. Buyers still compare your machine with boiling, which is free, so many still say no.
options.why: You can't beat free on price. Even a cheaper machine costs more than boiling, and now each sale earns you less. Remember: when they say "too costly", ask "compared to what?"
options.better: Keep the price, and show what boiling really costs in fuel, time and doctor's bills. Then your price looks fair.
options.takeaway: In the 1980s you tried to beat free on price. You needed to show the value instead.

d3.title: After the sale

setup.text: It is the 1990s. Thousands of homes now own your purifier, but your price cut leaves little money in each sale. Every machine must be fitted to a tap, and its filter wears out. Your salespeople are paid mostly for new sales, so they want to move on to the next door.

It is the 1990s. Thousands of homes now own your purifier, and your team spends hours collecting monthly payments. Every machine must be fitted to a tap, and its filter wears out. Your salespeople are paid mostly for new sales, so they want to move on to the next door.

It is the 1990s, and thousands of homes now own your purifier. Every machine must be fitted to a tap, and its filter wears out. Your salespeople are paid mostly for new sales, so after one sale they want to move on to the next door.

d3.question: What happens after a machine is sold?
d3.advisor: Every hour spent on an old customer is an hour not spent finding a new one. And new sales are what pay our people.

options.label: Keep salespeople focused on new sales, and let local mechanics fit and repair the machines.
options.outcome: Sales keep coming, but local mechanics fit machines badly and use cheap filters. When the water tastes odd, families blame your name and tell their neighbours.
options.why: The sale is not the end. A family that trusts your service buys filters, repairs and the next machine from you. Remember: a customer is worth the margin on all their future buys.
options.better: Fit every machine yourself, send technicians back regularly, and sell yearly service plans.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you walked away after the sale and left your name in a stranger's hands.

options.label: Repair machines only when owners call, and charge a fee for every visit you make.
options.outcome: You earn a little on each call. But most owners call only after the machine has failed, and by then some have gone back to boiling. Few buy a second machine from you.
options.why: Waiting for the call means you only turn up when something has gone wrong. Regular visits keep the machine working and the family buying. Remember: a customer is worth the margin on all their future buys.
options.better: Fit every machine yourself, send technicians back regularly, and sell yearly service plans.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you waited for customers to call. Regular care could have kept more of them buying.

options.label: Fit every machine yourself and send technicians back regularly, even though you need many more staff.

outcome.text: A company plumber fits every purifier, and your technicians return to service it. You open labs to test water and sell yearly service plans. By 2012, close to 9 million Indian homes are your customers.

A company plumber fits every purifier, and your technicians return to service it. You also sell yearly service plans. Families who trust your service keep buying filters and plans from you, year after year.

options.why: A machine sold once can earn for years through filters and service. Remember: a customer is worth the margin on everything they buy from you, not just the first sale.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you looked after every machine you sold, and families kept buying from you.

text.text: It is 2005. Your sales team has grown to thousands of young people trained to show the machine and close a sale. Most of their pay is commission. Since your price cut, each sale pays them less, so many good sellers leave.
It is 2005. Your sales team has grown to thousands of young people, paid mostly by commission. But in many towns, your name now means a badly fitted machine, so doors close faster than before.

It is 2005. Your sales team has grown to about 5,300 people, most in their mid-twenties. Each person gets three weeks of training: how to dress, how to show the machine, and how to close a sale. Most of their pay is commission, and after six months or 60 sales, they earn a motorbike.

d4.title: What does one sale cost?

setup.text: It is 2012. Your share of purifier sales has slipped from three in four to about six in ten. Rivals sell cheaper machines in shops. More families now live in gated buildings, where guards stop your salespeople at the gate. About 7,500 of your people still knock on doors.

It is 2012. Rivals sell cheaper machines in shops, and your share of purifier sales is slipping. More families now live in gated buildings, where guards stop your salespeople at the gate. Your large door-to-door team costs more every year.

d4.question: How do you sell from now on?
d4.advisor: Here is a rough sum using made-up round numbers: if one salesperson costs us ₹20,000 a month and sells ten machines, that is ₹2,000 of selling cost in every sale. But those home visits are also why families trust us.

options.label: Hire thousands more salespeople and knock on more doors, even if your pay bill rises.
options.outcome: Your pay bill jumps, but guards keep many new salespeople at the gate. Each extra sale costs more than the last, so the money left from each one keeps shrinking.
options.why: More knocks only help if each sale earns more than it cost to win. Remember: each customer must earn you more than you spent to win them.
options.better: Work out what one sale costs in each channel. Keep home demos where they pay, and put simpler models in shops.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you hired more sellers without doing the sums. Each customer must earn more than they cost to win.

options.label: Check the cost of each sale and put simpler models in shops, even if some sellers leave.
options.outcome: Your sums show that a home visit pays off for costly machines, but not for basic ones. You put simple models in shops and keep demos for the rest. Your sales team shrinks, and some loyal sellers leave angry, but each sale now costs you less.
options.why: Remember: know what it costs to win one customer. The way that made you famous isn't always the cheapest way to reach the next buyer.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you did the sums on every sale and changed how you sold, even though it hurt.

options.label: Keep door-to-door sales at the core, but use online ads to bring in demo requests.
options.outcome: You decide not to break up your sales force because it is the core of the company. Online ads now bring in requests for demos. In 2014 you still have more than 8,000 salespeople, while rivals keep selling in shops.
options.why: A demo that a family asked for is easier to close, so online ads were a smart fix. But every sale still paid for a home visit, and buyers who shop in stores never met you. Remember: know what it costs to win one customer.
options.better: Work out what one sale costs in each channel. Keep home demos where they pay, and put simpler models in shops.
options.takeaway: In 2012 you kept your famous sales team at the centre. You still needed to check what every sale cost.

legend.title: A name every home trusts
legend.text: You keep the home visits that made your name and sell simpler machines in shops. Each sale now earns more than it costs. Families who first met your salesperson at the door now buy your filters in shops and online, and Aquaguard stays the word India uses for a water purifier.

text.text: For about 25 years, your salespeople built a name India trusted for clean water. Then cheaper rivals in shops took ground. New owners since 2021 also sell through shops and online, and by 2025 sales at the door are about a quarter of the total.
Your big sales team keeps the brand alive, but every sale costs more each year. Rivals sell cheaper machines in shops, and your lead slowly slips away.
You fix how you sell in the end, but earlier mistakes cost you years. Your brand survives, while rivals in shops keep much of the lead you could have had.
You build a brand many families know, but not every sale earns its keep. Rivals in shops catch up, and your lead slowly slips away.

collapse.title: Lost at the door
collapse.text: Families never come to trust your name. Rivals with cheaper machines in shops win the homes you tried to reach, and your company shrinks to a small player.

fired.title: The owners lose faith
fired.text: After three costly calls, the owners lose faith in you and bring in a new chief to run the company.

realHistory: Eureka Forbes began in 1982 as a joint company of the Tata group's Forbes & Company and Sweden's Electrolux. It sold its Euroclean vacuum cleaners in homes, not shops, and in the 1980s added Aquaguard, India's first water purifier. From one Bombay office with 20 salespeople in 1987, its door-to-door team grew to more than 8,000 by 2014. It talked many families out of boiling water, and Aquaguard held three in four purifier sales in 2004–05. A company plumber fitted each machine, technicians came back to service it, and service became a big, steady income. Then gated buildings, cheaper rivals and shops ate into its lead: its share fell to about six in ten by 2012. Under new owners since 2021, it sells through shops and online too; by 2025 direct sales were about a quarter of the total.
